planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring against a sturdy trellis, fence, or arbor in well-drained soil; Dragon Lady is a more compact, restrained grower than the wild species, making it easier to keep in bounds.

directions: Grow in rich, well-drained soil in full sun for the heaviest bloom, though this native evergreen vine tolerates part shade with somewhat reduced flowering. Dragon Lady bears an unusually dark burgundy-red trumpet flower with a bright yellow throat in mid-spring, a striking color break from the orange tones of most crossvine selections, and semi-evergreen foliage that takes on wine-red tints through winter. It climbs by twining tendrils tipped with adhesive discs, so it self-clings readily to wood, brick, or wire without staking once established. Prune immediately after the spring flush to control size and remove any dead wood, and expect visits from hummingbirds drawn to the tubular blooms.

planting.note: Plant container vines in spring on a fence, trellis, arbor, or pergola in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Shalimar Red reblooms in summer and fall in addition to its main spring flush.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, giving this vigorous, fast-growing native vine a sturdy structure to self-cling to with its adhesive tendril discs. Shalimar Red is valued for deep coral-red, lightly fragrant, trumpet-shaped flowers that open heaviest in spring but continue sporadically into summer and fall, a longer season of bloom than many crossvine selections offer. Foliage takes on attractive reddish-purple tones in cool fall weather before the semi-evergreen leaves persist through a mild winter. Cut back after the main spring bloom to keep growth in check and encourage branching, since this is a fast, dense grower capable of quickly covering a large arbor or fence.

planting.note: Plant container vines in spring against a fence, arbor, or trellis in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this selection derives from the wild dark-flowered form of crossvine found in the Gulf South.

directions: Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for the deepest flower color, though the vine tolerates woodland-edge part shade. Atrosanguinea is a selection of the naturally occurring dark-flowered variety of crossvine, bearing narrow, deep purplish-red trumpet flowers with a contrasting yellow throat in mid-spring, a moodier, richer color than the orange-flowered forms more commonly sold. The glossy, semi-evergreen, twice-compound leaves persist through winter in the Gulf Coast climate, turning maroon in cold snaps. It climbs by clinging tendrils and needs no tying once established; prune right after flowering to control its vigorous size on a permanent structure.

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade on a fence, trellis, or arbor; this Proven Winners selection blooms over a long season from spring into summer.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade, providing a fence, arbor, or trellis for the self-clinging tendrils to grip. Dressed to Thrill is a Proven Winners ColorChoice introduction bred for a longer bloom window than older crossvine selections, opening fiery red-orange, trumpet-shaped flowers with a bright yellow throat continuously from spring into summer rather than in a single spring flush. The dense, glossy, semi-evergreen foliage provides good year-round screening on a fence or pergola, and the extended nectar supply draws steady hummingbird and butterfly traffic through the growing season. Prune lightly after the heaviest early bloom to shape the vine and keep it within its allotted space.

common_name: Pale Yellow Carolina Jessamine (Woodlander's Pale Yellow)

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring on a mailbox post, fence, or trellis in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; this selection is less cold-hardy than typical Carolina jessamine and best suited to zone 8 and warmer.

directions: Grow in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, training the twining stems onto a trellis, fence, or mailbox post. Discovered as a wild selection in the Florida panhandle and introduced by Woodlanders Nursery, Pale Yellow bears larger, soft primrose-yellow trumpet flowers rather than the deep golden yellow of the typical species, a subtler color for gardeners who want the fragrance and evergreen habit of Carolina jessamine without the bright gold. It flowers heaviest in late winter into early spring and carries the same sweet fragrance as the species. Because it is somewhat less cold-hardy than seed-grown Carolina jessamine, site it in a sheltered spot at the northern edge of its range, and keep in mind that all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant container vines in spring on a trellis, fence, or arbor in well-drained, average soil in full sun to part shade; Butterscotch flowers later than typical Carolina jessamine and reblooms again in fall.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to part shade, and provide a trellis, fence, or arbor for the twining stems to climb. Butterscotch is a drought- and heat-tolerant Carolina jessamine selection that delays its main flush of bright yellow, sweetly fragrant, bell-shaped flowers two to three weeks later than the species in late winter to early spring, then surprises with a second round of bloom in fall when few other vines are flowering. Its medium-green, glossy foliage stays neat and evergreen through the growing season, and the narrower habit compared to seedling Carolina jessamine makes it a good fit for a mailbox post or narrow trellis. Prune lightly after the spring bloom to control size, and remember that all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.
